body_text: View All News Alto Neuroscience Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Recent Business Highlights August 12, 2026 – ALTO-207 development expanded: an additional Phase 3 trial evaluating ALTO-207 as monotherapy in treatment-resistant depression (TRD) is now planned, alongside the ongoing potentially registrational Phase 2b trial; topline Phase 2b data on track for 2H 2027 – – Independent investigator-led study results published in Nature Medicine reinforce the dopaminergic mechanism underlying ALTO-207, demonstrating significant effects on anhedonia (Hedges' g=0.62, p=0.006) – – Approximately $100 million financing completed in July 2026; pro forma cash of approximately $338 million expected to fund planned operations through 2030 – MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Alto Neuroscience, Inc. (“Alto”) (NYSE: ANRO), a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on the development of novel precision medicines for neuropsychiatric disorders, today reported financial results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, and highlighted recent progress across its pipeline of clinical-stage product candidates. “The second quarter further strengthened the case for ALTO-207 and our conviction in the opportunity ahead of it,” said Amit Etkin, M.D., Ph.D., founder and chief executive officer of Alto Neuroscience. “The Nature Medicine publication of PRIME-PRAXOL provides another independent, peer-reviewed dataset showing that dopaminergic treatment produces large effects in depression, and, just as importantly, a reminder of the tolerability challenge that ALTO-207 is designed to address. With enrollment in our potentially registrational Phase 2b trial tracking as planned and pro forma cash of approximately $338 million, we are now positioned to pursue ALTO-207 in both the adjunctive and monotherapy settings, broadening the potential label and the commercial opportunity, with expected runway through 2030.” Second Quarter and Recent Pipeline Highlights ALTO-207: Independent Nature Medicine publication reinforces mechanism; monotherapy Phase 3 trial added to development plan ALTO-207 is a fixed-dose combination of pramipexole, a dopamine D3-preferring D3/D2 agonist with demonstrated antidepressant effect across multiple independent trials, and ondansetron, a selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist. The fixed-dose combination is designed to enable rapid titration to higher pramipexole doses by mitigating the dose-limiting nausea and vomiting associated with pramipexole. This combination approach — and its use to enable higher pramipexole dosing in the treatment of depression — is the subject of Alto's issued method-of-treatment patent estate described below. ALTO-207 is being developed to address the significant unmet medical need in TRD, which is estimated to affect approximately 7 million adults in the United States. In June 2026, results from PRIME-PRAXOL — an independent, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted by investigators at Lund University, Sweden — were published in Nature Medicine. Adults with major depressive disorder (MDD), dysthymia, or bipolar depression and clinically significant anhedonia received flexible-dose pramipexole or placebo added to ongoing treatment for nine weeks, followed by a six-month open-label extension. The trial met its primary endpoint, with pramipexole reducing anhedonia significantly more than placebo on the Snaith–Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS) (mean difference −4.04; 95% CI −6.89 to −1.18; p=0.006; Hedges' g=0.62). Significant improvements were also observed on independent measures of anhedonia (DARS; p=0.008) and apathy (AES-S; p<0.001), and improvements were maintained through the six-month open-label period. In an exploratory analysis included in the publication, an MDD diagnosis was significantly associated with greater SHAPS improvement at week 9 relative to dysthymia (p=0.038). In an additional analysis of the trial data not included in the publication, the MDD subgroup showed a larger effect on SHAPS at week 9 (Hedges' g=0.99) and a larger effect on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS-6) (Hedges' g=0.64). Consistent with prior studies, adverse events were common in the pramipexole arm despite slow titration, including nausea in approximately 60% of participants — the dose-limiting tolerability constraint that the ALTO-207 fixed-dose combination is designed to address. These findings are consistent with the broader body of evidence supporting ALTO-207, including the PAX-D study conducted by the University of Oxford and published in The Lancet Psychiatry (Cohen's d=0.87 versus placebo at 12 weeks in TRD) and a meta-analysis of pramipexole in depression (Hedges' g=0.64, p<0.001). The broad development program for ALTO-207, collectively the PACE program ( P ramipexole-ondansetron A ssessment of C linical E fficacy in depression), remains on track across three large, well-controlled clinical trials; PACE-1 Trial (Phase 2b adjunctive TRD trial): Enrollment in the ongoing, potentially registrational, Phase 2b trial of ALTO-207 as an adjunctive treatment in approximately 178 adults with TRD is on track with topline data expected in 2H 2027. MADRS is the primary endpoint in the trial, which is aligned with FDA standards in depression and supports the potential for the trial to contribute to a future registrational package alongside the planned Phase 3 trials. PACE-2 Trial (Phase 3 adjunctive TRD trial): Alto remains on track to initiate its Phase 3 trial of ALTO-207 as adjunctive treatment in TRD by early 2027, following alignment with the FDA on the planned trial design. title: What FinCEN’s Beneficial Ownership Reporting rollback means
summary: FinCEN ended beneficial ownership reporting for U.S. companies and will delete 15 million domestic-company reports. See what changes for banks and investigators.
body_text: 01 Overview FinCEN’s final rule ended beneficial ownership information reporting for companies formed in the U.S. on August 14, 2026. The agency will also delete 15 million reports from domestic companies that it received before it added a reporting exemption for U.S. businesses in March 2025. The rule removes the standardized federal ownership record Congress intended to create for financial institutions and investigators. Banks still have customer-due-diligence responsibilities, and investigators still need to identify the people behind a business. They will rely more heavily on customer submissions, state filings, commercial sources, and investigative tools that were never designed to function as one system. Middesk helps institutions assemble the remaining evidence into a clearer business identity by connecting records from more than 400 government sources across all 50 states with submitted information and other business indicators. Middesk then normalizes those records, weighs the strength of matching evidence, and links them into a source-backed identity graph that teams can use to verify, investigate, monitor, and make decisions about a business. In brief: FinCEN ended beneficial ownership reporting for U.S.-formed companies and kept narrower reporting requirements for certain foreign-formed companies registered to do business in the United States. The final rule relieves an estimated 27.5 million outstanding or expected domestic-company filings and eliminates about 53 million hours of annual reporting work and $9 billion in modeled annual compliance costs. Banks and investigators still need ownership information, but they will have to reconcile more customer submissions, state records, commercial sources, and investigative data without one federal ownership record for U.S.-formed companies. 02 What FinCEN’s final rule changes The Corporate Transparency Act created a federal reporting system for beneficial ownership information, which identifies the individuals who own or control a company. The system was intended to give authorized law enforcement agencies and financial institutions with customer consent access to a standardized ownership record. Before the agency introduced a broad domestic-company exemption in March 2025, it received approximately 15 million reports from domestic reporting companies. The final rule makes that exemption permanent and U.S.-formed companies no longer have to file beneficial ownership reports with FinCEN. Foreign-formed companies registered to do business in the United States remain reporting companies, but they do not have to report the beneficial ownership information of U.S. persons or company applicants. U.S. persons likewise do not have to provide that information to those companies. FinCEN estimates that the narrower regime relieves approximately 27.5 million outstanding or expected domestic-company filings. The agency expects approximately 16,800 foreign reporting companies in the first year and about 1,800 new reporting companies in each subsequent year. 03 Why banks still need ownership information Financial institutions still have to comply with customer due diligence responsibilities. They can still collect ownership information directly from customers. They can ask a business to provide ownership details, verify those details through other sources, and use the results when assessing the customer’s risk. Banks will have to do more of that work without a federal record for U.S.-formed companies. State filings vary in what they collect, how often businesses update the information, and who can access it. A filing may list officers, directors, managers, or members without identifying the people who own or control the business. The Bank Policy Institute last year supported reducing unnecessary reporting burdens but warned that the narrower approach could shift more work to businesses and banks. Financial institutions may need to request ownership information more often and reconcile it across less consistent sources. 04 How Middesk helps teams assemble a business identity The loss of federal beneficial ownership information adds complexity by distributing that information across state systems that are not standardized and have different definitions, update cycles, and levels of detail. Middesk makes fragmented evidence more usable and gives teams a clearer record of what the available sources show, where they agree or conflict, and what still requires review. Middesk connects state registrations and other government records with submitted business information, and analyzes the connections between businesses and people. Its entity resolution engine normalizes those records, weighs the strength of matching evidence, and links related records into a source-backed business identity. That identity powers structured verification results, review insights, risk scores, investigation findings, policies, and ongoing monitoring. Banks, fintechs, lenders, and other institutions can compare what a customer submitted with available records, surface inconsistencies, and route exceptions for further investigation. The Government Accountability Office also found that state records vary in the ownership and control information they collect. Some may identify an officer, director, manager, or member without identifying the people who own or control the business. Investigators can use subpoenas, suspicious activity reports, customer records, and commercial databases, but those sources do not create one complete, standardized record of company ownership. Deleting domestic-company beneficial ownership information removes a stable federal reference point. Investigators will have to compare more records across jurisdictions, organizations, and time to determine whether the information identifies the same business and people. The Government Accountability Office recommended that Treasury identify ways to address the risks created by the expanded exemptions and provide Congress and law enforcement with useful information about those risks. title: Destination Databricks 4.0: Up to 4.5x Faster with Direct Loading and Speed Mode
summary: Destination Databricks 4.0 is up to 4.5x faster with Direct Loading, Speed Mode, and Avro staging, cutting sync time and warehouse compute costs.
body_text: With Destination Databricks 4.0.0, we've reworked the connector's data path end to end — from the source container all the way into your Delta tables. Syncs now run up to 4.5x faster on larger datasets while leaning on less warehouse compute. Three changes drive it: Speed Mode , a faster parallel transport between containers; Direct Loading , which writes typed data straight into final tables; and a migration onto Airbyte's new Bulk CDK framework. This is the latest stop in a rollout that's already reached Snowflake , BigQuery , and Redshift . Databricks is one of the most heavily used destinations on the platform, so moving it onto the same modern pipeline was a priority. What follows walks through the architecture changes, the parts of your setup that don't move, and where the benchmarks landed. What Changed in 4.0.0 Five changes define this release: Speed Mode — A socket-based transport replaces JSON-over-stdio with Protobuf-over-Unix-domain-sockets, opening parallel data channels between the source and destination containers. Direct Loading — The connector writes typed data directly to final tables, eliminating the intermediate raw tables and the Typing and Deduping SQL overhead that came with them. Avro staging format — Staging files move from CSV + gzip to Avro + Snappy, so data arrives already typed and the warehouse no longer infers schema or casts on load. Schema evolution — Column adds, drops, and type changes are handled with granular ALTER TABLE and CTAS operations instead of v3's full-table rebuild. Bulk CDK migration — The connector is rebuilt on Airbyte's new Bulk CDK framework with Micronaut dependency injection, standardizing the loading pipeline and improving parallelism. Speed Mode, Direct Loading, and the Bulk CDK migration are covered in depth in separate posts; here we focus on how they come together for Databricks, along with the two destination-specific changes — Avro staging and schema evolution detailed below. Speed Mode: What It Means for Databricks Speed Mode redesigned how data moves between containers in Airbyte's architecture. The details are covered in our engineering deep-dive , but here's the short version for Databricks syncs. Before (v3.x): Data flowed from source to orchestrator to destination through standard I/O pipes. Every record was serialized as JSON, parsed by the orchestrator, re-serialized, and parsed again by the destination. The orchestrator sat in the middle of every byte of data. After (v4.0.0): Records flow directly from source to destination over multiple Unix domain sockets, serialized as Protocol Buffers. A lightweight Bookkeeper replaces the orchestrator, handling only control messages (logs, state, metadata). The data channel never touches the Bookkeeper. For Databricks specifically, this matters because: Parallel Volume uploads: Multiple data channels feed Avro files into Unity Catalog Volumes simultaneously, keeping the staging pipeline saturated. Optimized batch sizing: Files are aggregated into ~250MB batches, tuned for Databricks COPY INTO performance. Reduced serialization overhead: Protobuf's binary format with column-value arrays (instead of repeated key-value JSON) cuts both CPU usage and bytes on the wire. Direct Loading: No More Raw Tables In previous versions, Destination Databricks used a two-step process called Typing and Deduping: write untyped JSON to a raw table ( _airbyte_raw_{stream} ), then run SQL — get_json_object to extract fields, cast types, and MERGE into the final table. The raw tables never stopped growing. Each sync appended to previous data, and Databricks ran transformation SQL on every sync, so compute costs climbed over time. With Direct Loading, the connector handles type-casting in-memory before data reaches Databricks. Typed records are written directly to final tables — no persistent raw tables, no transformation SQL in your warehouse. The loading path still stages through Unity Catalog Volumes and loads with COPY INTO , and deduplication is still handled by MERGE INTO on the final table. What changed is what gets loaded, which is the next section. Avro Staging: Typed Files Instead of JSON-in-CSV The staging format moved from CSV + gzip to Avro + Snappy — and this is what makes raw tables unnecessary. In v3, every record was dumped into a raw table as a single JSON blob in _airbyte_data , with all type information flattened to strings. Databricks then had to infer schema on load ( inferSchema=true ), extract fields with get_json_object() , and cast them in SQL. That path was slow and bug-prone — inferSchema guessed INT32 for _airbyte_generation_id where the column was BIGINT, forcing an explicit cast workaround inside a COPY INTO subquery. In v4, the connector does all type work in the JVM and writes typed Avro: each field becomes its own column with a native Avro type, and the schema travels inside the file. Databricks knows every type at load time — no inference, no extraction, no casting. The COPY INTO collapses from a wrapped subquery with three format options to a single line: SQL -- v3: the CSV file format with inferSchema computation enabled COPY INTO `catalog`.`raw_ns`.`_airbyte_raw_stream` FROM ( SELECT _airbyte_generation_id :: bigint , * except (_airbyte_generation_id) FROM '/Volumes/.../file.csv.gz' ) FILEFORMAT = CSV FORMAT_OPTIONS ( 'header' = 'true' , 'inferSchema' = 'true' , 'escape' = '"' ); SQL -- v4: the Avro schema handles everything COPY INTO `catalog`.`namespace`.` table ` FROM '/Volumes/.../file.avro' FILEFORMAT = AVRO; On compression, Snappy replaces gzip: a slightly larger file in exchange for much cheaper compression and decompression. For a staging file that lives for seconds before COPY INTO, throughput beats compression ratio. Combined with the typed-on-write design, the format change pulls work out of both phases that dominate sync time — staging and loading — and eliminates a class of CSV escaping and type-inference bugs along the way. Schema Evolution: v3 vs v4 Schema changes are where v3 and v4 differ most. When a source adds a column, changes a type, or drops a field, the two versions take fundamentally different paths. v3 — full-table soft reset. v3 has no incremental schema evolution; there are zero ALTER TABLE statements in the codebase. On a schema mismatch it rebuilds the whole table: create a temp table with the new schema, clear every load marker in the raw table ( _airbyte_loaded_at = NULL ), re-run Typing and Deduping over every historical record , then atomically swap the temp table in. For a table with millions of rows, one new column means reprocessing everything — expensive in both time and Databricks compute. v4 — granular operations. v4 implements the CDK's TableSchemaEvolutionClient with three targeted operations: Add column — ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN (preceded by a delta.feature.timestampNtz property when adding a TIMESTAMP_NTZ column). No reprocessing. Drop column — ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN , after enabling delta.columnMapping.mode = 'name' . Existing data is untouched. Type change — an atomic CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT that casts the changed column in place: SWIFT CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE `catalog`.`schema`.`table` AS SELECT `_airbyte_raw_id`, `_airbyte_extracted_at`, `_airbyte_meta`, `_airbyte_generation_id`, `retained_col`, CAST (`changed_col` AS STRING ) AS `changed_col`, CAST ( NULL AS STRING ) AS `new_col` FROM `catalog`.`schema`.`table`; For adds and drops — the common case — evolution is a metadata-only operation that completes near-instantly regardless of table size. Only true type changes re-scan the final table, and there's no raw table to reprocess from. What Stayed the Same Upgrading from v3.x to v4.0.0 is designed to be straightforward. Several core behaviors are unchanged: Same configuration: No changes required. (The one removal is raw_schema_override , which no longer applies now that there are no raw tables.) Unity Catalog Volumes staging with COPY INTO: Data is still staged via Volumes and loaded with COPY INTO. Authentication: Both OAuth (M2M) and Personal Access Token are still supported. All sync modes: Full refresh (overwrite/append) and incremental (append/dedup) behave as before. What Else Improved Configurable CDC Deletion: Soft or Hard Delete v4 adds a cdc_deletion_mode option. v3 only supported hard deletes — a deleted source row was removed from the destination with no trace. v4 lets you choose: hard delete (default, preserves existing behavior) or soft delete , which retains the row as a tombstone with _ab_cdc_deleted_at set. Soft delete fits when you need an auditable deletion history or want downstream logic to react to delete events. It's a per-connection setting. Library Upgrades Library v3 v4 com.databricks:databricks-jdbc 2.6.40 3.3.3 com.databricks:databricks-sdk-java 0.31.0 0.110.0 The JDBC driver jump from 2.6.40 to 3.3.3 brings improved connection stability, better Unity Catalog support, and eliminates the --add-opens JVM workarounds v3 required. The SDK upgrade brings improved Volume operations and OAuth support. Robust Connection Checker The pre-flight check is now an end-to-end mini-sync: it creates a table, writes Avro through the full pipeline, runs COPY INTO, verifies the row count, and cleans up. Misconfigurations surface before the sync starts, not midway through. Value Coercion and Validation Integer overflow (INT64 range) and decimal precision (28 integer digits for DECIMAL(38,10)) are checked before load. Out-of-range values are nulled with metadata recorded in _airbyte_meta.changes — visibility instead of silent corruption or a failed sync. Higher Parallelism A multi-threaded aggregate pipeline buffers 250MB per aggregate, 1GB total, up to 5 buffered aggregates, maximizing throughput across multiple streams. Improved Test Suite New component tests cover schema evolution, data coercion, and table operations, with Protobuf/socket acceptance tests running alongside the existing JSONL/stdio paths. Updated Spec and Docs The spec is now annotation-driven with inline doc links (replacing hand-written JSON), and fields are reorganized into clearer groups: connection, sync behavior, and advanced. Benchmarks Scenario v3 (MB/s) v4 (MB/s) Improvement Default — 1 GB 8.04 13.10 +62.9% Boosted — 1 GB 16.08 25.97 +61.5% Default — 10 GB 9.54 42.47 +345.2% Boosted — 10 GB 15.74 66.45 +322.2% We benchmarked v3 (latest) against v4.0.0 using 1GB and 10GB datasets on both default and boosted Databricks configurations. The improvement scales with data volume. On smaller 1GB syncs, where fixed startup overhead dominates, v4 is roughly 1.6x faster. On 10GB syncs the architectural wins take over: throughput jumps from 9.54 to 42.47 MB/s on default configurations (4.5x) and reaches 66.45 MB/s on boosted ones (4.2x). The gains come from every layer working together — faster data transfer (Speed Mode), less work in the warehouse (Direct Loading), a lighter staging format (Avro + Snappy), and a more efficient loading pipeline (Bulk CDK). Migration Guide Upgrading to 4.0.0 This version upgrades Destination Databricks to the Direct Loading paradigm. If you have specific requirements around record visibility or schema evolution, review the Direct Loading documentation for how it differs from Typing and Deduping. If you do not interact with raw tables , you can upgrade safely. There is no breakage for this use case. If you interact with raw tables (downstream dbt models, SQL queries, or dashboards that reference _airbyte_raw_* tables), follow these steps: Update any downstream dbt models or SQL queries to reference the final tables instead of raw tables. Upgrade the destination to version 4.0.0. Verify data in the final tables after the first successful sync. (Optional) Drop old raw tables ( _airbyte_raw_* ) after verifying the new tables contain the expected data. The deadline to upgrade to v4 is 2026-10-01 . What's Next If you're running Databricks with Airbyte, you'll get these improvements automatically when you upgrade to v4.0.0. If you're not yet on Airbyte, try it free and see the difference.

title: Why Private Equity Firms are Turning to Pooled Employer Plans
summary: Private equity firms found a smarter way to handle retirement plans across their portfolios. See how one model cuts risk, cost, and administrative strain.
body_text: Private equity firms spend significant time helping portfolio companies improve operations, reduce risk, and create scalable infrastructure. Retirement plans are often overlooked in that process, yet they can create administrative complexity, fiduciary exposure, audit costs, and inconsistent governance across a portfolio. A Pooled Employer Plan (PEP) offers an alternative model that can help private equity sponsors standardize retirement plan oversight while reducing burdens on portfolio company leadership. What is a Pooled Employer Plan? Created under the SECURE Act, a Pooled Employer Plan lets multiple employers participate in a single, professionally managed 401(k) plan. Rather than each company managing a plan on its own, key administrative, compliance, and investment responsibilities move to experienced fiduciaries. That shift reduces the burden on participating employers while keeping oversight strong. Why Private Equity Firms are Looking at PEPs Private equity firms are drawn to Pooled Employer Plans because they replace scattered, company-by-company oversight with one centralized model. That shift matters because portfolio companies often run on lean teams, yet each one acts as its own fiduciary. A small internal team ends up handling plan administration, coordinating audits, managing several provider relationships, and keeping pace with compliance rules that never stop changing. Repeat that across a portfolio, and a retirement plan becomes a source of administrative complexity, fiduciary risk, and compliance burdens. A PEP shifts that work away from individual companies and brings retirement oversight into the same efficiency strategy sponsors apply across the portfolio. Key Benefits for Private Equity Portfolio Companies Reduced Fiduciary Risk A PEP moves the key fiduciary responsibilities to dedicated specialists who take them on by design. That handoff gives portfolio companies a clearer, more structured governance framework and far less personal exposure to carry. Lower Administrative and Audit Burden Plan administration runs more efficiently when one coordinated team handles it. The pooled structure also consolidates audits at the plan level, which cuts the disruption and compliance demands that usually fall on each company, so management teams can get back to running the business. Cost and Operational Efficiencies Pooling many employers into one plan unlocks economies of scale that a single company cannot reach on its own. Processes get streamlined across the portfolio, vendor coordination shrinks, and administrative overhead drops along with it. A Valuable Tool for Mergers and Acquisitions Growth through acquisition is core to how private equity firms operate, and every deal brings another company with its own 401(k) to fold in. A PEP gives sponsors a ready-made framework to bring newly acquired businesses on board without untangling and rebuilding a plan each time. It also creates consistency across the portfolio, so companies share one plan structure as they grow, acquire, or prepare for an exit. A single audit and faster plan setup can even smooth the closing itself, cutting the friction that legacy plans sometimes drag into a deal. In a Pooled Employer Plan, unrelated companies participate in one professionally managed 401(k), and a Pooled Plan Provider takes on most of those duties, including regulatory filings and investment oversight. The PEP structure standardizes many plan features across participating employers, which helps create consistency, streamline administration, and capture economies of scale while still allowing for certain employer-specific provisions. Not entirely, and it is worth being clear on this. A PEP shifts most fiduciary duties, including investment management and day-to-day administration, to the Pooled Plan Provider, allowing management to focus on operating the business rather than administering a retirement plan. The participating employer keeps one core responsibility: prudently selecting and monitoring the provider. So a PEP does not erase fiduciary duty. It narrows the employer’s role to selecting the provider and monitoring performance. Acquisitions often mean inheriting a company’s existing 401(k), along with its compliance history and administrative work. A PEP gives sponsors a clean, ready-made structure to fold new companies into quickly, sometimes in as little as 60 days. title: Strengthening Health Plan Collaboration to Improve Claims Accuracy and Patient Access
summary: Learn how GeneDx Clinical Billing Integrity supports accurate genetic testing claims through medical necessity review, documentation, coding, credentialing, and payor collaboration.
body_text: Key Takeaways GeneDx’s Clinical Billing Integrity team brings together clinical, coding, credentialing, contract operations, and revenue cycle expertise to support billing integrity across the genetic testing claim lifecycle. Establishing medical necessity and providing required clinical documentation early can help health plans make more informed coverage decisions upfront. Accurate CPT/ICD-10 coding and alignment with payor requirements can help reduce denied claims, repeated documentation requests, and administrative rework. GeneDx’s proactive approach is designed to prevent billing issues before they occur while supporting timely access to medically necessary genetic testing. ‍ How Clinical Billing Integrity Supports Genetic Testing Claims In molecular pathology and genetic testing, accurate claims processing is essential to both patient access and administrative efficiency. When prior authorizations or claims are incomplete, misaligned with policy, or submitted without the right documentation, the result can be denied claims, avoidable appeals, and delays in care. At GeneDx, the Clinical Billing Integrity (CBI) team was built to address these challenges proactively, serving as a bridge between clinical excellence and revenue cycle performance to ensure claims are accurate, well-supported, and aligned with payor expectations from the start. A Cross-Functional Approach to Billing Integrity What makes the CBI team distinctive is its cross-functional foundation. It's led by genetic counselors with experience in both direct patient care and large payor organizations, a combination that brings deep understanding of the clinical context behind genetic testing and the policy frameworks that guide coverage decisions . CBI also includes experienced medical coding professionals, contract operations specialists, and payor credentialing experts. Together, these disciplines move billing beyond a traditional "bill and appeal" model toward one built on accuracy, transparency, and upfront alignment. Getting Genetic Testing Claims Right the First Time The CBI team's mission is twofold: help patients access their insurance benefits for medically necessary testing and reduce administrative burden for GeneDx and payor partners alike. That starts with establishing medical necessity as early as possible, ideally before a claim is ever generated. By educating ordering providers on exactly what documentation payors require, GeneDx can submit clinical records earlier, often during prior authorization, giving health plans what they need to make informed coverage decisions upfront. Coding accuracy is equally critical. Molecular pathology coding is highly specialized, and GeneDx's coding experts ensure testing is represented in line with payor expectations and CPT/ICD-10 standards, helping guarantee internal systems reflect accurate pricing, contract terms, and coding requirements. Together, this upfront rigor reduces denied claims, repeated documentation requests, and lengthy appeals. Supporting Billing Integrity Across the Claim Lifecycle The CBI team's strength lies in supporting billing integrity at every stage: Clinical Billing Integrity Analysts conduct medical necessity reviews and apply payor clinical policies to inform billing strategy. Medical Coding Professionals support precise diagnosis reporting and accurate procedural coding. Credentialing Experts verify providers and services are properly enrolled with payors, reducing administrative delays. Revenue Cycle Contracts Management oversees fee schedules, payor contracts, and test menu alignment, so internal systems reflect payor structures accurately. Together, these functions help GeneDx prevent issues upfront instead of resolving them after they occur. A More Collaborative Path Forward for Health Plans GeneDx is committed to being a responsible, collaborative partner to health plans. Through accurate coding, comprehensive documentation, and clear contractual alignment, the Clinical Billing Integrity team helps support timely patient access to medically necessary genetic testing, while enabling health plans to make faster, better-informed coverage decisions. The partnership gives CPG brands a direct path to 7-Eleven and Speedway shoppers through the Ibotta Performance Network, with brands only paying when there is a verified sale of their product. This partnership expands Ibotta’s footprint into the convenience channel, bringing the accountability CPG brands rely on in grocery and delivery to one of the largest loyalty ecosystems in the market. title: Amazon Quick adds deny by default for custom permissions
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with Amazon Quick adds deny by default for custom permissions
body_text: Amazon Quick custom permissions now include deny by default, a governance setting that automatically restricts new AI capabilities before they reach users. Previously, new AI capabilities were available to all users on release, requiring administrators to react after the fact. With deny by default, administrators restrict the AI capability category in a custom permissions profile and assign it to users, roles, or the entire account. Quick then denies any new AI capability at launch for those users. Restricting a category also restricts existing capabilities in it. Administrators explicitly allow each capability when ready. The restriction applies only to the profile you configure. Configure deny by default in Manage account in Amazon Quick or through the AWS CLI. To learn more, see Custom permissions deny by default . Deny by default is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Quick is available .

title: How to Build Agents That Work in Private Equity Environments
summary: Everyone wants to talk about models. The hard part of deploying agents across a PE firm is everything else: mapping every workflow by role, deciding who owns each step, and redesigning the firm so humans and agents actually work together.
body_text: Most of what gets written about building agents is about the technology. This piece is about everything else: the non-coding part of building enterprise-ready agents that need to be deployed across private equity, and what the partnership between firms and agent vendors has to look like for any of it to work. Start with workflow mapping The crucial first step, one that I harp about a lot, is workflow mapping. Map out all workflows in the organization, separated by roles and groups. The way to do this is simply to look through the chronological steps of each job to be done for each function in the company. For example, a VP of business development at a private equity firm will look at how he takes a deal from the first time he hears about it to handing it off to the M&A team for further diligence. That usually requires multiple steps: analyzing the teaser, processing the NDA, requesting supplementary information, creating a one-pager, meeting and prepping with the banker for an intro call on the deal, logging all of it into the CRM, and then packaging everything up for the Monday morning new deals review meeting. This is by no means a completely linear process. The deal could be originated from a banker in our network on a quarterly catch-up call, an outbound email in a niche sub-sector we are looking to develop a thesis in, or a net-new broker we have never spoken with. Each makes the process slightly different and creates hundreds of nuances along the way. Agent vendors have to pick a niche and go deep enough in it that these edge cases are covered a few months into implementation for the first few clients, and in a few weeks for most future clients. The devil truly does lie in the details. A live example I understand this can be quite abstract to imagine, so let's take a live mock example from what we see on the daily. We are on a quarterly catch-up call with our guy at Harris Williams. He mentions a DSO based in Arizona coming to market in five months, not giving us much more than a revenue and EBITDA range and a couple of points on the ownership. Currently, this is one of the 30 things he mentions on the call. A Head of BD somewhere in New York or London is probably jotting it down in OneNote and creating a reminder to reach back out about the opportunity in a few months. That is also the optimal case. Investors don't do all of this for every new deal opportunity, because it simply takes too much manual work today. The same call, redesigned around agents In a collaborative workspace, redesigned for human PE investors to co-work with agents, here is how that same situation plays out. Prior to the quarterly catch-up, Zarna's agent gathers context from its memory on the relationship, which is a synthesis of data that lives in systems like DealCloud, SharePoint, Box, the Outlook inbox, PitchBook, and web data. A brief can contain a variety of details that would previously have slipped through the cracks. An example: "these are the three deals Matt from Harris Williams said would be coming live around Labor Day across our last four conversations with him, here is the background on each, along with a one-liner on potential fit at our firm." The agent will also pull up a transaction announcement from PitchBook that Matt was on last week that would have fit our criteria but we never got a look at. The list goes on. So far, pretty agent-led. The call is yours to dictate and own. You control the flow. This part is human-led. Our agents connect to your note-taker, whether that is Granola, the Zoom notetaker, or manual notes stored in a folder, and post-meeting they port all of it into your CRM and our reminder system with action items from the conversation. One action item might be connecting Matt at HW with one of our deal partners to discuss an interesting portco add-on opportunity. Another might be checking on a specialty chemicals teaser that should come out in two weeks. Zarna's agent drafts that email and creates that reminder, with the draft ready to go. No human input required; you press send. Agent-led, human behind the wheel for the final decision. Bridge the gap before you deploy Figuring out how to align your business processes for cohesion between agents and humans is what you need to crack as a firm. This is a joint effort between the organization itself and the agent vendor it decides to go with. Usually, organizations will have done some work beforehand and have some ideas. But agent vendors have seen what has worked and what hasn't across the industry, and have a much better understanding of what an agent is going to be able to do and not, at least off the bat. The two teams have to work together to bridge that gap before deploying anything. The playbook 1. Map out all workflows in the organization, separated by roles and groups, by walking the chronological steps of each job to be done. 2. Map out who leads and decides what at each step: the owner. Do not overlook this step, and make sure there is internal agreement between key stakeholders. Ownership is critical to understand. Who the agent is reporting to matters more than you think. 3. Make a decisive call on whether each step should be human-led (deciding whether to reach out to an expert the agent suggested), agent-led (one-pager creation), completely human (speaking at IC), or completely agentic (CRM and file storage entry). 4. Redesign your firm workflows and redistribute the work. 5. Design and launch agents. 6. Run agent and human evals. Is our thesis shaping up correctly? Is the agent outperforming the human where it should be? Is the human outperforming the agent where he should be? If not, rethink the division of labor. 7. Track KPIs: number of new deals sourced, number of bids placed. These are all learnings from several years of building agents for complex enterprise environments, for clients with no appetite for risk in output or performance. Thanks for reading. title: Automotive Drilling: How Manufacturers Improve Consistency — MSC Industrial Supply Co.
summary: While drilling is a mature machining process, maintaining consistency at scale remains a significant challenge for many manufacturers.
body_text: Drilling operations are at the core of high-volume automotive manufacturing. From powertrain components to chassis and safety parts, millions of holes are produced every year under demanding conditions. While drilling is a mature machining process, maintaining consistency at scale remains a significant challenge for many manufacturers. This article explores common automotive drilling challenges and highlights process-focused best practices used to improve stability and repeatability in production environments. Why drilling performance matters in automotive manufacturing In automotive production, drilling is rarely performed in isolation. Hole quality directly affects downstream operations such as reaming, tapping, assembly, and functional performance of the finished component. Variability in drilling can therefore have a cascading impact on throughput, quality metrics, and overall manufacturing cost. Common drilling challenges in high-volume automotive production Despite standardized production lines, automotive manufacturers frequently encounter similar drilling-related issues: 1. Inconsistent hole size, position, or surface quality over long production runs As precision standards rise, maintaining hole dimensional accuracy, roundness, and surface finish has become more demanding than ever. Automotive components such as cylinder heads, transmission housings, and braking systems often require micron-level tolerances, making stable precision drilling and finishing processes essential. Factors like tool deflection, vibration, and machine instability can negatively affect hole quality. To address this, manufacturers rely on rigid setups, high-performance coatings, and stable tool holding systems. Additionally, multi-step operations, combining drilling, chamfering, and counterboring, can improve efficiency but increase process complexity. High-quality indexable and solid carbide drills with optimized geometries help ensure consistent performance across varying materials and machine conditions. 2. Chip evacuation problems in deep, cross, or interrupted holes A key challenge in drilling lies in the variation of cutting speed across the drill diameter, dropping to zero at the center, which adds to process complexity. This is why carefully engineered drill geometries are critical for ensuring efficient chip evacuation and consistent performance. One of the most persistent issues in automotive drilling is chip management. Whether deep hole drilling in engine blocks or producing shallow features in chassis components, uncontrolled chips can clog flutes, increase friction, and damage surface finishes. Effective chip control depends on tool geometry, coolant strategy, and cutting parameters. For chip control in drilling, features such as optimized helix angles, polished flutes, and through-coolant designs play a crucial role in maintaining a clean cutting zone. Modern drills with through-coolant capabilities deliver high-pressure fluid directly to the cutting edge, stabilizing temperatures and ensuring consistent chip evacuation, especially vital in automated production lines where downtime directly impacts productivity. 3. Tool wear variation caused by material inconsistencies or changing cutting conditions The shift toward lightweighting and electrification has transformed the material landscape. Components once made primarily from cast iron or steel now incorporate aluminum alloys, advanced high-strength steels (AHSS), and composites – each bringing unique drilling challenges. In practice, this often means switching between drilling aluminum and drilling AHSS within the same plant, sometimes within the same assembly. Aluminum alloys demand high cutting speeds and efficient chip evacuation to prevent built-up edges. AHSS generates high heat, accelerating tool wear. Composites pose risks such as delamination and fiber pullout if parameters are not optimized. These complexities require specialized drill geometries, advanced coatings, and carefully tuned cutting parameters. Optimized flute design and point angles help reduce cutting forces and improve surface integrity – especially critical in multi-material assemblies. 4. Tool life vs. cycle time: high-speed drilling wear challenges in automotive manufacturing Automotive production lines are built for high throughput, leaving little room for unplanned stops. While tool wear is inevitable, minimizing its impact is essential for maintaining productivity and controlling costs. Heat generation, cutting forces, and coating performance all influence tool life. Incorrect parameter selection can significantly reduce tool longevity, leading to inconsistent results, more tool changes, and higher cost per hole. Advancements such as nanostructured coatings, optimized edge preparations, and material-specific geometries are enabling longer tool life – even under high-speed or dry machining conditions. The objective is clear: maximize productivity while ensuring consistent hole quality and reducing overall tooling costs. 5. Automation & Industry 4.0: drilling process monitoring and integration challenges With the rise of smart manufacturing and Industry 4.0, drilling operations are increasingly integrated into automated, data-driven systems. While automation improves efficiency, it also introduces new challenges: Variations in workpiece positioning or material batches can affect tool performance. Predictive maintenance requires accurate data from sensors and tool monitoring systems. Adaptive machining strategies depend on consistent and repeatable tool behavior. Modern drilling solutions must go beyond cutting, they must integrate seamlessly into digital manufacturing environments. Sensor-enabled tooling and predictive analytics are helping manufacturers monitor tool performance in real time, anticipate wear, and optimize process stability. Process-focused best practices for improving drilling stability Rather than relying on a single change, manufacturers typically improve drilling performance through a combination of process-oriented actions. These often include careful alignment of tool geometry with application requirements, consistent pre-hole conditions, and monitoring wear behavior to avoid unexpected failures. Establishing stable, repeatable cutting conditions is generally prioritized over pushing maximum performance limits. The importance of standardization in automotive drilling processes Standardization plays a critical role in reducing variation across machines, shifts, and production sites. Clearly defined machining parameters, documented setups, and controlled tool change intervals help ensure that drilling results remain predictable over time. In high-volume environments, this level of consistency is essential for maintaining quality while controlling cost per part. Building reliable drilling processes for long-term performance Automotive drilling challenges are largely driven by scale, repetition, and the demand for zero-defect production. By focusing on process stability, repeatability, and standardized practices, manufacturers can reduce variability and support continuous improvement across their drilling operations. Understanding these fundamentals is a critical first step toward evaluating more detailed application, or solution-specific approaches. Quick checklist to improve automotive drilling performance Validate chip evacuation with the right flute design and coolant delivery (especially for deep hole drilling). Control hole quality by managing runout, rigidity, and vibration in the full holemaking sequence. Balance tool life and cycle time with material-specific parameters for drilling aluminum and drilling AHSS. Use process monitoring (spindle load, vibration, coolant pressure) to reduce variation on automated lines. Precision, efficiency, and reliability: the three pillars of modern automotive production, all begin with a perfect hole. This article was previously featured on Seco's blog .

title: Eficiencia empresarial: cómo alinear objetivos, personas y resultados
summary: La eficiencia empresarial ya no se trata de exigir más esfuerzo, sino de alinear mejor.
body_text: Durante mucho tiempo, la eficiencia empresarial se asoció casi exclusivamente con hacer más en menos tiempo. Reducir costos, aumentar la productividad y exigir mayor esfuerzo parecían ser las fórmulas principales para mejorar los resultados. Sin embargo, en el contexto actual, esta visión resulta limitada y, en muchos casos, contraproducente. ‍ Hoy, las organizaciones operan en entornos complejos, cambiantes y altamente competitivos, donde el trabajo del conocimiento, la colaboración y la innovación son claves. En este escenario, la eficiencia ya no depende únicamente de trabajar más horas o de exigir más a las personas, sino de alinear correctamente los objetivos estratégicos con el trabajo diario de los equipos y con los resultados esperados . ‍ Cuando esa alineación no existe, surgen problemas conocidos: esfuerzos dispersos, baja claridad de prioridades, colaboradores desmotivados y estrategias que no se ejecutan como se planearon. En cambio, cuando los objetivos están bien definidos, son comprendidos por todos y cuentan con seguimiento continuo, la eficiencia organizacional aumenta de forma sostenible. ‍ Este artículo explica qué es la eficiencia empresarial desde una mirada moderna, por qué la falta de alineación reduce su impacto y cómo las organizaciones pueden mejorarla conectando objetivos, personas y resultados. Además, se incluyen ejemplos prácticos de alineación organizacional y se muestra cómo plataformas como Lapzo permiten integrar estos elementos en un solo sistema. ‍ Qué es la eficiencia empresarial ‍ La eficiencia empresarial suele confundirse con productividad, pero no son lo mismo. La productividad se centra en la relación entre insumos y resultados: cuántos recursos se utilizan para generar un determinado output. La eficiencia, en cambio, incorpora una dimensión adicional: el uso inteligente y alineado de esos recursos para lograr los objetivos correctos . ‍ Una organización puede ser productiva y, aun así, ineficiente. Por ejemplo, equipos que trabajan intensamente, cumplen tareas y entregan resultados, pero que no contribuyen de manera significativa a los objetivos estratégicos del negocio. En estos casos, hay esfuerzo, pero no necesariamente impacto. ‍ La eficiencia empresarial implica priorizar bien, enfocar los esfuerzos donde generan mayor valor y evitar el desperdicio de energía en actividades que no aportan a los resultados esperados. ‍ Relación entre eficiencia, personas y resultados ‍ En las organizaciones modernas, la eficiencia está profundamente ligada a las personas. Son ellas quienes interpretan los objetivos, toman decisiones, ejecutan tareas y resuelven problemas. Sin una conexión clara entre lo que la empresa busca lograr y lo que las personas hacen cada día, la eficiencia se diluye. ‍ Cuando los colaboradores entienden cómo su trabajo impacta en los resultados, tienden a priorizar mejor, a comprometerse más y a tomar decisiones alineadas con la estrategia. Por el contrario, cuando esa relación no es visible, el trabajo se fragmenta y pierde sentido. ‍ Por eso, hablar de eficiencia empresarial hoy implica hablar de alineación , claridad , participación y seguimiento , más que de control o presión. ‍ Por qué la falta de alineación reduce la eficiencia ‍ Objetivos desconectados del trabajo diario ‍ Uno de los principales factores que afectan la eficiencia es la desconexión entre los objetivos estratégicos y el trabajo cotidiano de los equipos. En muchas organizaciones, los objetivos se definen a nivel directivo, pero no se traducen adecuadamente en acciones concretas para los distintos roles. ‍ Esto genera situaciones en las que los colaboradores no saben con claridad qué se espera de ellos o cómo sus tareas contribuyen al resultado global. Como consecuencia, se prioriza lo urgente sobre lo importante y se pierde foco en lo que realmente genera valor. ‍ La falta de alineación provoca que cada equipo avance en direcciones diferentes, reduciendo la eficiencia global de la organización. ‍ Bajo involucramiento de los colaboradores ‍ Cuando los objetivos se imponen sin considerar la perspectiva de los equipos, el involucramiento disminuye. Las personas tienden a comprometerse menos con metas que no entienden, no comparten o sienten ajenas a su realidad diaria. ‍ Este bajo involucramiento impacta directamente en la eficiencia. Sin compromiso, aumenta la resistencia al cambio, se reduce la iniciativa y se limita la capacidad de los equipos para adaptarse y mejorar. ‍ En cambio, cuando los colaboradores participan en la definición y seguimiento de los objetivos, se sienten parte del proceso y asumen mayor responsabilidad sobre los resultados. ‍ Esfuerzos sin impacto real ‍ La falta de alineación también genera esfuerzos que no producen impacto. Proyectos que consumen tiempo y recursos, pero que no mueven los indicadores clave del negocio. Reuniones, reportes y tareas que se realizan por inercia, sin cuestionar su aporte real. ‍ Este tipo de ineficiencia no siempre es visible a simple vista, pero afecta profundamente la capacidad de la organización para ejecutar su estrategia y adaptarse al entorno. ‍ Cómo alinear objetivos, personas y resultados ‍ Definición clara de objetivos ‍ El primer paso para mejorar la eficiencia empresarial es definir objetivos claros, concretos y bien comunicados. Los objetivos deben ser comprensibles para todos los niveles de la organización y estar directamente vinculados a la estrategia. No se trata solo de definir qué se quiere lograr, sino también de explicar por qué es importante y cómo se medirá el éxito. La claridad en los objetivos permite que las personas prioricen mejor y enfoquen sus esfuerzos de manera más eficiente. Un ejemplo práctico es el uso de objetivos claros y medibles a nivel de equipo, alineados con objetivos organizacionales, que facilitan la toma de decisiones en el día a día. ‍ Participación de los equipos ‍ La alineación no se logra únicamente desde arriba hacia abajo. Involucrar a los equipos en la definición y ajuste de los objetivos mejora significativamente la eficiencia. Cuando las personas participan, aportan información valiosa sobre la viabilidad de las metas y se comprometen más con su cumplimiento. ‍ La participación también permite adaptar los objetivos a la realidad operativa, evitando metas poco realistas o desconectadas del contexto. ‍ Organizaciones que promueven conversaciones abiertas sobre objetivos logran mayor coherencia entre estrategia y ejecución. ‍ Seguimiento continuo del progreso ‍ Definir objetivos no es suficiente. La eficiencia mejora cuando existe un seguimiento continuo del progreso, que permita detectar desviaciones, ajustar prioridades y reconocer avances oportunamente. ‍ El seguimiento frecuente evita sorpresas al final del período y facilita la toma de decisiones basada en datos. Además, refuerza la sensación de avance y propósito en los equipos. ‍ Este enfoque transforma los objetivos en herramientas vivas, que guían el trabajo diario y no en simples declaraciones formales. ‍ Errores comunes al buscar eficiencia empresarial ‍ Enfocarse solo en métricas ‍ Uno de los errores más habituales es reducir la eficiencia a un conjunto de métricas, sin considerar el contexto ni el comportamiento de las personas. Si bien los indicadores son necesarios, cuando se convierten en un fin en sí mismos pueden generar efectos negativos. ‍ Las métricas mal diseñadas o mal comunicadas pueden incentivar comportamientos contrarios a la eficiencia real, como priorizar el número sobre la calidad o cumplir objetivos individuales en detrimento del resultado colectivo. La eficiencia empresarial requiere métricas relevantes, pero también conversaciones y análisis cualitativos. ‍ Sobrecargar de objetivos ‍ Otro error frecuente es definir demasiados objetivos al mismo tiempo. La sobrecarga de metas genera confusión, dispersa los esfuerzos y reduce la capacidad de los equipos para enfocarse. ‍ Cuando todo es prioritario, nada lo es. La eficiencia mejora cuando las organizaciones aprenden a priorizar y a concentrarse en pocos objetivos clave, claramente alineados con la estrategia. ‍ Falta de visibilidad ‍ Sin visibilidad sobre los objetivos y su avance, la alineación se debilita. En muchas organizaciones, la información sobre metas y resultados está fragmentada, lo que dificulta el seguimiento y la colaboración entre equipos. ‍ La falta de visibilidad impide identificar bloqueos, duplicidades de esfuerzo y oportunidades de mejora, afectando directamente la eficiencia. ‍ Cómo Lapzo ayuda a mejorar la eficiencia empresarial ‍ Alineación de objetivos ‍ Lapzo permite definir y alinear objetivos organizacionales, de equipo e individuales en un solo sistema. Esta alineación facilita que cada colaborador entienda cómo su trabajo contribuye a los resultados globales, mejorando el foco y la priorización. ‍ La conexión clara entre niveles de objetivos reduce la dispersión y fortalece la coherencia estratégica. ‍ Seguimiento en tiempo real ‍ La plataforma ofrece visibilidad en tiempo real del avance de los objetivos, lo que permite a líderes y equipos monitorear el progreso, detectar desviaciones y ajustar acciones de manera oportuna. Este seguimiento continuo elimina la necesidad de revisiones aisladas y mejora la capacidad de reacción de la organización. ‍ Conexión con desempeño y desarrollo Lapzo integra los objetivos con la gestión del desempeño y el desarrollo de las personas. De esta forma, la eficiencia no se mide solo en resultados, sino también en la evolución de las competencias y el crecimiento de los equipos. Esta conexión asegura que el logro de objetivos vaya acompañado de aprendizaje y mejora continua, fortaleciendo la eficiencia de forma sostenible. ‍ Conclusión ‍ La eficiencia empresarial ya no se trata de exigir más esfuerzo, sino de alinear mejor . Alinear objetivos claros con el trabajo diario de las personas, fomentar su participación y dar seguimiento continuo al progreso son factores clave para lograr resultados sostenibles. ‍ Las organizaciones que logran esta alineación reducen esfuerzos innecesarios, aumentan el compromiso y mejoran su capacidad de ejecución estratégica. title: Best VoIP phone system for small business in 2026
summary: Six VoIP phone systems for small business, compared on pricing, AI features and hidden fees, so you pick the right one the first time.
body_text: TL;DR We recommend Google Voice for solo founders and freelancers on a tight budget, because the personal plan is free and the $10/user Starter plan covers the basics without asking for a long-term commitment. We recommend LinkedPhone for small US and Canada-based teams who want a shared inbox for calls, texts, and voicemails without juggling three separate apps. We recommend Allo for small teams and sales teams who want AI baked into every plan (not an add-on) and CRM integrations that actually sync call recordings and transcripts. We recommend Dialpad for growing SMBs (think 20 to 200 people) who want a phone system with genuinely strong built-in AI. We recommend Zoom Phone for small businesses already living inside Zoom's ecosystem and who want their phone, meetings and chat under one login. We recommend Microsoft Teams Phone for Microsoft 365 shops willing to accept a more complex setup process in exchange for keeping calls inside Teams. Introduction Picking a phone system used to mean picking a desk phone. Now it means picking a stack: calling, texting, an AI receptionist, CRM sync, and (hopefully) a bill you can predict. We tested and reviewed six VoIP phone systems built for or adopted by small businesses: Google Voice, LinkedPhone, Allo, Dialpad, Zoom Phone and Microsoft Teams Phone. Some are dedicated small business tools; others are the phone add-on to a suite you might already use. None of them fit every team the same way. This guide walks through what each one does well, where it falls short, what it actually costs once you add the fees nobody puts on the pricing page, and how to think about the switch to VoIP if you haven't made it yet. Summary table Tool Recommended to Starting monthly price G2 rating iOS rating Play Store rating Google Voice Solopreneurs and Google Workspace users on a budget Free (personal) / $10 per user (business) 4.1/5 4.3/5 1.8/5 LinkedPhone Small US/Canada teams wanting a unified inbox $19.99/month (1 user) 3.5/5 4.7/5 3.8/5 Allo Small teams and sales teams wanting AI + CRM sync, no add-ons $16/month (1 user, Starter) 4.7/5 4.3/5 3.9/5 Dialpad Growing SMBs wanting strong built-in AI $27/user/month 4.4/5 4.6/5 3.2/5 Zoom Phone Teams already using Zoom $18/user/month 4.6/5 Not published separately* Not published separately* Microsoft Teams Phone Microsoft 365 shops $10/user/month (tech only, calling plan extra) 4.4/5 4.8/5 4.5/5 *Zoom's App Store rating covers the combined Zoom Workplace app, which includes Zoom Meetings, so it isn't Zoom Phone specific. Google Voice: the free option that stays basic Google Voice is the phone system most people have already touched, even if they didn't think of it that way. It's free for personal use tied to a Gmail address, and it's the reason a lot of solo consultants and side-hustlers never bothered shopping for anything else. For actual business use, Google offers a Starter plan at $10 per user per month (up to 10 users, available in 14 countries), a Standard plan at $20 per user per month (unlimited users, on-demand call recording, call routing), and a Premier plan at $30 per user per month (automatic call recording, advanced reporting via BigQuery). Business plans require a Google Workspace subscription on top, which is easy to overlook when comparing raw prices. The catch is the feature set. Google Voice only has two AI features: spam blocking and voicemail transcription. There's no AI receptionist, no call summaries, no CRM integrations of any kind. If your business runs on HubSpot or Salesforce, you'll be logging calls by hand. What we'd flag before you buy: No customer support on the free personal version. Business use is limited to the US, Canada and a short list of supported countries. You can't always port an existing US number over. Bottom line: Google Voice makes sense if your needs are simple (a working number, basic voicemail, and a price you'll never think twice about) and you don't need the phone system to talk to the rest of your tools. LinkedPhone: one inbox for calls, texts and voicemail LinkedPhone, started in 2017 by a small NYC based team, leans hard into the "everything in one shared inbox" pitch. Calls, texts, voicemails and emails between team members show up in a single place, with text auto-reply and missed call auto-reply built in. Pricing is tied to number type rather than a traditional tiered plan: a local number runs $19.99 per month for one user, a toll-free number runs $29.99, and each additional user is $5 per month on either plan. There's a 7-day free trial and, refreshingly, no add-ons layered on top. AI features are limited but free across the board: AI reply suggestions, call transcription and voicemail transcription. That's a smaller set than what Allo or Dialpad offer, but at least you're not paying extra for it. What we'd flag before you buy: LinkedPhone only works in the US and Canada, has no CRM integrations beyond Zapier, and while we haven’t had any issues ourselves, a few online reviews mention frequent bugs. There's also no HIPAA compliance, which rules it out for healthcare-adjacent businesses. Bottom line: a fair pick for a small, US-based team that wants one inbox and doesn't need CRM sync, international coverage or heavy AI. Allo: AI phone system built mobile-first for small teams Allo is built specifically for small teams and salespeople rather than retrofitted from an enterprise product. Where Allo stands out is how much AI ships in the base experience: an AI answering service (in French, Spanish or English), call transcription and summaries across 36 languages, automatic follow-up email drafts, and an AI assistant you can ask questions of using your own call transcripts and SMS history as the source. All of it is included in the plan price. There's no separate AI add-on to negotiate, which is unusual on this list; most competitors charge extra for their AI receptionist. The other differentiator is CRM depth. Allo has 18 native integrations, including HubSpot , Salesforce, Pipedrive, Attio, Notion, Zoho CRM and Apollo, and they sync call recordings, transcripts and contact updates back into the CRM rather than just logging that a call happened. Its HubSpot integration holds a 5/5 rating on the HubSpot marketplace across 200-plus installs, which is high compared to most tools on this list. Pricing: the Starter plan is $16 per month for a single user (requires a 1-year commitment) and includes unlimited calls, a local number, AI summaries and IVR. The Business plan is $45 per user per month and unlocks integrations, unlimited AI answering, SMS and international calls. One phone number is included; extra numbers cost $5 per month. Cancellation is self-serve, no questions asked, and there's a 7-day free trial. What we'd flag before you buy: integrations and the full AI receptionist are gated behind the Business plan, so the $16 Starter tier is closer to a solo-user option than a team plan. Being newer, Allo also may not suit large enterprises with complex, multi-department routing needs; call routing itself (simultaneous or cascade) is available only on Business. Bottom line: if AI and CRM sync are the reason you're switching phone systems in the first place, Allo is worth shortlisting, especially for sales teams who live in their CRM. Dialpad: the AI-first pick for growing teams Dialpad's AI credentials go back further than most: founder Craig Walker previously built GrandCentral, the product Google acquired and turned into Google Voice. That shows up in the feature set: call summaries, live coaching, call scoring and an AI support agent, all included free across plans and supporting 9 languages. Dialpad also runs three separate products (Connect, Support, and Sell) aimed at general use, support teams and sales teams respectively, each with its own pricing. The Standard plan starts at $27 per user per month and includes unlimited calling within your home country plus the US and Canada, a local number, call forwarding, recording and up to 3 departments for call routing. The Pro plan is $35 per user per month and adds SSO, phone support and up to 25 departments. A 14-day free trial is available. What we'd flag before you buy: several reviewers point to call quality issues and a steeper learning curve than a tool like Google Voice or LinkedPhone. Support response times also come up repeatedly in reviews, and the SMS approval process can be slower than expected. Bottom line: a solid choice for a business between roughly 20 and a few hundred employees that wants AI coaching and analytics without paying a per-feature add-on tax, as long as you're prepared for a real onboarding curve. Zoom Phone: the natural add-on if you already use Zoom Zoom Phone launched in 2019 to sit alongside the video product most small businesses already know. If your team runs meetings on Zoom, adding Zoom Phone means one login, one app and one bill instead of stitching together a separate VoIP provider. AI features are branded as "AI Companion" and include post-call summaries, voicemail transcription, voicemail task extraction, voicemail prioritization and SMS thread summaries, supporting 32 languages. The catch: the more advanced summary and task features are included in every plan, but the full AI Companion experience is reserved for the Pro Plus and Business Plus tiers. The entry plan, US & CA Unlimited, is $18 per user per month and includes unlimited domestic calling, free SMS, a phone number, call recording and integrations (Salesforce and Slack among others). Pro Plus bundles in the full Zoom Workspace suite (Meetings, Team Chat, Docs, Mail) for $24 per user per month, and Business Plus adds more storage, larger meeting capacity and SSO for $29 per user per month. The free trial (7 days) only applies to the entry plan. What we'd flag before you buy: Zoom Phone's HubSpot integration has a notably low 1.9/5 rating on the HubSpot marketplace across 179 reviews, and reviewers call out missing shared contacts on the mobile app plus a short onboarding window. Compared to Allo or Dialpad, Zoom Phone's AI answering capabilities (no true AI receptionist or AI IVR) are thinner. Caption: If you use HubSpot, Zoom phone will probably not be your best option Bottom line: makes the most sense as an add-on for teams that are already committed to Zoom for meetings, less so as a standalone phone system chosen on its own merits. Microsoft Teams Phone: powerful, but plan carefully Microsoft Teams Phone extends Teams into a full calling solution, with Copilot integration letting you ask questions during or after a call and get answers pulled from the transcript. The pricing structure is where this one gets complicated. Teams Phone Standard is $10 per user per month (paid yearly) but only covers the phone system technology itself, not calling minutes; you'll need a certified external provider or Microsoft's own calling add-ons for that. Teams Phone with pay-as-you-go calling is $13 per user per month, and Teams Phone with a Calling Plan (3,000 domestic minutes for the US, UK and Canada) is $17 per user per month. On top of that, you need a separate Microsoft Teams license starting at $4 per user per month, and the Copilot add-on for AI features costs another $30 per user per month. Add it all up and this becomes one of the more expensive options on this list, not the cheapest. What we'd flag before you buy: in our own testing, the setup process was genuinely confusing, requiring you to juggle Microsoft 365 admin settings and Teams Phone settings separately, often being told mid-setup that you need to buy a number first and starting the process over. This will likely require an IT admin to configure properly. CRM integrations also lag behind dedicated VoIP tools; the HubSpot integration sits at 3.3/5, and there's no native Salesforce integration. Bottom line: worth it if your business already runs on Microsoft 365 and you value keeping calls inside Teams more than you value a quick setup or a predictable monthly bill. Conclusion There's no single best VoIP phone system for every small business; the right pick depends on your budget, your existing tools, and how much you need AI to do the busywork for you. If your budget is close to zero and your needs are simple, Google Voice covers the basics. If you want one shared inbox for a small US-based team, LinkedPhone keeps things simple. If AI and CRM sync matter more than anything else, Allo and Dialpad both deliver, with Allo leaning toward small sales teams and Dialpad toward growing SMBs that want deeper analytics. If you're already committed to Zoom or Microsoft 365, Zoom Phone or Microsoft Teams Phone will save you from managing a separate app, as long as you go in with your eyes open about the added cost of AI features and integrations. Whichever you choose, read the pricing page twice: the sticker price rarely includes AI add-ons, extra phone numbers or the per-user minimums that show up once you start comparing plans side by side. ‍ FAQ What are the recommended phone systems for small businesses? Google Voice, Allo, Dialpad, Zoom Phone and Microsoft Teams Phone all serve small businesses, but they suit different situations. Google Voice fits the tightest budgets, Allo and Dialpad fit teams that want AI and CRM sync built in, and Zoom Phone or Microsoft Teams Phone fit businesses already using those ecosystems. How much does a small business VoIP phone system cost? Entry-level plans on this list range from free (Google Voice's personal plan) to around $27 per user per month (Dialpad's Standard plan). Most paid business plans land between $10 and $20 per user per month at the entry tier, with advanced AI features, CRM integrations or additional phone numbers often priced separately. Which criteria are critical when choosing a phone system? Three things matter most: integrations, AI features and total pricing. On integrations, check whether the tool actually syncs call recordings and transcripts into your CRM, not just a call log entry. On AI, check whether the AI receptionist and transcription are included in your plan or billed as a per-minute add-on, since several tools on this list charge separately for their AI answering service. On pricing, look past the advertised number for per-user minimums, extra phone number fees, and calling plan costs that aren't bundled into the base price. When is it recommended to switch to VoIP? Common triggers include outgrowing a personal cell phone for business calls, needing call recording or transcripts for a growing sales team, or wanting a single number that can ring multiple people at once.

title: Grab pilots AI-powered call service to make ride booking easier for seniors | Grab SG
summary: The Grab AI Call-A-Ride (Beta) is currently optimised for English and Chinese, with plans to expand to more regional languages. Through this pilot, Grab aims to gather feedback to refine and improve…
body_text: Others August 5, 2026 Grab pilots AI-powered call service to make ride booking easier for seniors The Grab AI Call-A-Ride (Beta) is currently optimised for English and Chinese, with plans to expand to more regional languages. Through this pilot, Grab aims to gather feedback to refine and improve the experience. Available via the phone number +65 3138 0000, Grab AI Call-A-Ride (Beta) enables ride booking via natural conversation with an AI voice assistant SINGAPORE, 5 August 2026 – Grab Singapore today announced the launch of Grab AI Call-A-Ride (Beta), an AI-powered call service for booking rides. Available via the phone number +65 3138 0000 , this pilot service enables ride booking via natural conversation with an AI voice assistant, empowering seniors and anyone who finds mobile app navigation challenging or inconvenient. Developed in collaboration with OpenAI and powered by its Realtime Voice model, the AI voice assistant is able to engage in fluid reasoning – it interprets intent, maintains context, adapts mid-sentence, and processes bookings unlike traditional automated call services. The Grab AI Call-A-Ride (Beta) solution is currently optimised for English and Chinese, with plans to expand to more regional languages. Through this pilot, Grab aims to gather feedback to refine and improve the experience. Philipp Kandal, Chief Product Officer at Grab, said: “Advancements in AI are enabling us to better solve a long-standing paradox: choosing between scale and accessibility. Years ago, live agent call services were easy to use but difficult to scale, while earlier efforts at voice automation often resulted in rigid, frustrating menus. The shift to apps unlocked massive scale, but didn’t work for segments of our community who struggle with digital navigation – often some of the very people who need reliable mobility the most. The Grab AI Call-A-Ride (Beta) seeks to bridge this divide. By integrating Grab’s proprietary speech technologies and hyper-local data with foundational voice models, we are trying to bring back the intuitive simplicity of a voice call, backed by the flexible reasoning and scalability of conversational AI – taking another step towards safe, reliable mobility for everyone.” Albert Yip, Head of Technical Success, Asia Pacific from OpenAI, added, “Grab’s service shows what becomes possible when advanced AI is designed around the real needs of the people it serves. By combining OpenAI’s Realtime Voice model with Grab’s deep understanding of its users, our teams are helping make ride booking more natural and accessible for seniors and visually impaired users. It’s a meaningful example of how close collaboration can bring the benefits of AI to more people in their everyday lives.” Prior to launch, the Grab AI Call-A-Ride (Beta) underwent an initial trial processing approximately 1,000 pilot calls with various demographic groups. Grab partnered with grassroots digital inclusion initiatives to invite participants to test the solution, including at seniors’ digital literacy workshops organised by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA)’s SG Digital Office (SDO), and by Temasek at its Community Day 2026. Early tester sentiment was encouraging, and with the feedback garnered Grab further enhanced the system’s speech recognition accuracy and conversational pacing. To enable better parsing of unique regional accents and mixed-language environments like “Singlish,” Grab integrated over 100,000 voice sample donations collected locally. Developing the AI-powered call service also led to several engineering breakthroughs. A common challenge for voice-based AI is background noise, which often drown out the user’s voice and confuse the system. To address this, Grab developed a voiceprint solution, where over multiple call interactions with a user, the AI gets better at isolating and “locking” into the user’s unique voice as well as filtering out background audio. AI is enabling new ways to meet people where they are. From Grab AI Call-A-Ride (Beta) to the Voice Assistant for the Visually Impaired, Grab continues to experiment and innovate to find new ways for people to access everyday services on their own terms.
